phonemes.desc: Voiceless glottal [h], as in English 'hill'; initial h is fully sounded in Old Norse.
Short close front rounded [y] — the vowel of German 'ü' or French 'tu'; Old Norse y, one of the sounds English later lost.
Voiced bilabial nasal [m], short [i], and the final nominative trill [r], lightly sounded after the vowel.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HÜ-mir' — round the lips as for 'oo' while saying 'ee' for the y; the final r is the light nominative ending, as in Icelandic.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Hymir, the giant of Hymiskviða and Gylfaginning; the etymology is uncertain, usually connected with ON hum 'darkness, dusk' — hence the traditional gloss 'dark one'.

kin.label: The þulur
kin.form: Hymir, kept in the metrical name-lists as an ordinary giant-heiti — a name the poetic tradition carried on its roster of the jötnar.

kin.label: Skaldic tradition
kin.form: The unnamed giant of Bragi's Ragnarsdrápa (9th c.), Þórr's terrified companion in the fishing-boat, conventionally identified as Hymir.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Hymir, unchanged in spelling — the modern language keeps both the y and the final -r.

pronunciation.note: Hymir is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. Only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input; the y the name does carry is one ASCII shares with Old Norse.

domains.title: Giant, Owner of Cauldron
domains.subtitle: The Host at Heaven's End, the Ox-Head Bait, and the Cup Broken on a Giant's Skull
domains.lead: Hymir is the sea-giant of Hymiskviða: the fierce host at the eastern edge of heaven whose herd feeds his hall, whose fishing-ground is the cold reach of the Élivágar, and whose treasure is the one thing the gods lack — the mile-deep cauldron in which Ægir could brew ale for all the Æsir at once.

cards.name: The Mile-Deep Cauldron
cards.desc: The roomy, hard-forged kettle Týr says his fierce father owns — a mile deep, the only vessel large enough to brew for all the gods.

cards.name: The Ox-Head Bait
cards.desc: The head of the black bull Himinbrjótr, torn off by Þórr for bait — the offering that drew the Miðgarðsormr up from the sea-floor.

cards.name: The Crystal Cup
cards.desc: Hymir's unbreakable drinking-cup, which no pillar could crack — smashed at last on the one thing harder: the giant's own skull.

cards.name: The Hall of Cattle
cards.desc: The giant's byre at heaven's end, where Þórr devoured two of the three oxen at supper and beheaded the finest for the fishing.

symbols.name: The mile-deep cauldron
symbols.meaning: The vessel of plenty the giants keep and the gods must win — hospitality's measure in the Eddic world

symbols.name: The ox-head bait
symbols.meaning: The price of the catch: the herd's finest head traded for the serpent that girdles the world

symbols.name: The cup broken on the skull
symbols.meaning: The giant's own hardness turned against his treasure — strength answering strength

symbols.name: The nine-hundred-headed grandmother
symbols.meaning: The monstrous ancestry of the giant-house, set against the golden-browed mother who hides the guests

mythology.lead: Hymir lives in one great poem and its prose retelling: Hymiskviða, the comic and terrible lay of the cauldron-quest, and Gylfaginning 48, where Snorri tells the fishing-trip for the Miðgarðsormr with all its sea-cold detail. It is Þórr's most famous adventure, and the giant is its immovable setting.

myths.title: The Demand for the Cauldron
myths.text: The Æsir had hunted and taken auguries from the blood, and saw that Ægir — called also Gymir — had brew-stuff in plenty. Þórr ordered the sea-giant to brew ale for the gods, and Ægir, to be rid of the demand, set an impossible price: first let them bring a cauldron a mile wide. Týr knew where one stood: east of the Élivágar lives the shrewd Hymir at heaven's end, and "my fierce father owns the roomy kettle, a mile deep." So Þórr and Týr drove to the giant's hall. There they met Týr's grandmother, loathsome, with nine hundred heads — and another woman, golden-browed, Týr's mother, who hid the guests under the great cauldron, for her husband was often cruel to visitors.

myths.title: The Host Comes Home
myths.text: Hymir came in from the hunting with the ice rattling in his beard. The pillar he looked toward burst apart; eight cauldrons crashed from the broken beam, and one hard-forged kettle came down whole. The guests came out, and the hall fed them: three oxen were slaughtered, and Þórr alone ate two before he slept. In the morning the giant eyed his thinned herd and told his guest they must fish for the next day's meal — Þórr might row out with him, if the little fellow dared the cold and the long pull to his fishing-ground.

myths.title: The Fishing for the Miðgarðsormr
myths.text: Asked for bait, Þórr went to the herd and wrenched the head from the black bull Himinbrjótr — Snorri calls him Himinhrjóðr. Hymir rowed hard, then harder, and still Þórr matched him, past the giant's own grounds into water he said was unsafe, where the serpent lies. Hymir pulled up two whales at once on his hooks; Þórr cast the ox-head overboard. The Miðgarðsormr gaped on the bait, the hook caught, and Þórr braced his feet through the bottom of the boat and hauled the serpent's head to the gunwale — the two glaring, the sea foaming, the boat nearly swamped — until the hammer struck and the serpent sank back into the sea. Hymir rowed home in gloomy silence.

myths.title: The Cup, the Skull, and the Carrying-Off
myths.text: Back on land Hymir demanded proof of strength, and set his crystal cup: break that, and be counted mighty. Twice Þórr hurled it through the stone pillars, and twice it came back to the giant's hand unbroken — until the fair counsellor whispered to strike it on Hymir's own skull, harder than any cup. The cup shattered. Hymir mourned it with the formula of loss: he could no longer say over it "ale is brewed." Then, sullen, he yielded the wager — take the cauldron, if you can carry it out. Týr heaved twice and could not shift it; Þórr hoisted it over his head and strode off with the rim ringing at his heels. They had not gone far before he looked back and saw Hymir coming east from the caves with a troop of many-headed giants; he set down the cauldron, raised Mjöllnir, and slew the whole host. One of Þórr's goats went lame on the road — Loki's doing, the poem says — but the cauldron came to Ægir, who brews ale in it for the Æsir ever after.

lore.syncretism: Hymir's poem has drawn comparatists for a century because the cauldron-quest is one of the old travelling stories of the North Atlantic: a vessel of plenty, kept by a grudging power beyond the sea, won for the feast of the gods. Scholars since Dumézil have set Hymiskviða beside the Celtic cauldron-quests — the Welsh Preiddeu Annwfn, where Arthur sails for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, and the Irish cauldrons that no company leaves unsatisfied — and beside Vedic parallels for the winning of the gods' drink. The fishing scene has its own comparative trail: the thunder-god's combat with the sea-serpent belongs with the wide Indo-European dragon-fight. Inside the Norse corpus the neater tension is genealogical: Hymiskviða makes the giant Týr's father, while Snorri elsewhere counts Týr among Óðinn's sons — two filiations the tradition never reconciled.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hymir's afterlife is carried almost entirely by the fishing-trip, which became the most retold of all Þórr's adventures: Victorian mythographies made it a set-piece, modern handbooks open their Þórr chapters with it, and every popular retelling keeps the ox-head, the glaring serpent, and the giant rowing home in silence. In scholarship the poem holds a double distinction — it is both the fullest portrait of a giant household in the Edda and the standing exhibit in the debate over the cauldron-quest's Celtic kin. The name itself stayed where the þulur put it: a giant-name, rarely borrowed, carried into modern fantasy and games chiefly as the surly host of the world's most famous fishing story.
lore.extendedMeditation: Hymir is the Edda's portrait of hospitality under strain: the host who feeds his guests two oxen and counts the cost, who rows farther than he means to because pride will not let him ship his oar first, who wagers his treasures on contests he frames himself — and loses both. The poem never makes him a monster; it makes him a householder with a monstrous ancestry and a mile-deep kettle, and lets the comedy and the cold do the work. What the story measures is not his failure but the difference between keeping plenty and sharing it: the cauldron that brews for all the gods spent its best years in a hall where even a guest's supper was tallied.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Hymir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᚢᛘᛁᛦ (h-u-m-i-R, the ᚢ rune covering the rounded y and ᛦ writing the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: hymir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Orchard, Cassell's Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend

lore.archaeology: Hymir is a textual figure: his attestations are the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), which alone preserves Hymiskviða, and the manuscripts of Snorri's Edda; the þulur keep his name among the giant-heiti. The myth's antiquity is proven by skaldic verse: Bragi Boddason's Ragnarsdrápa (9th c.) describes the fishing-scene on a painted shield — the ox-head bait, the hooked serpent, the hammer raised — with the giant aboard conventionally identified as Hymir. The picture-record follows: the Altuna runestone (U 1161, Uppland) shows Þórr with his foot braced through the boat's bottom and the serpent on the line, and the Gosforth Cross fishing-panel shows two figures in the boat — the angler and his giant companion. No cult site, toponym, or inscription names Hymir himself.
